title: Carathéodory kernel theorem
intro: In mathematics, the Carathéodory kernel theorem is a result in complex analysis and geometric function theory established by the Greek mathematician Constantin Carathéodory in 1912. The uniform convergence on compact sets of a sequence of holomorphic univalent functions, defined on the unit disk in the complex plane and fixing 0, can be formulated purely geometrically in terms of the limiting behaviour of the images of the functions.

title: Cardioid
intro: In geometry, a cardioid (from Greek  καρδιά (kardiá) 'heart') is a plane curve traced by a point on the perimeter of a circle that is rolling around a fixed circle of the same radius. It can also be defined as an epicycloid having a single cusp.

title: Carleman's inequality
intro: Carleman's inequality is an inequality in mathematics, named after Torsten Carleman, who proved it in 1923 and used it to prove the Denjoy–Carleman theorem on quasi-analytic classes.

title: Carmichael function
intro:
In number theory, a branch of mathematics, the Carmichael function  λ(n) of a positive integer  n is the smallest positive integer m such that

am≡1(modn)
holds for every integer  a coprime to  n. In algebraic terms,  λ(n) is the exponent of the multiplicative group of integers modulo  n.

title: Carnot's theorem (thermodynamics)
intro:
Carnot's theorem (English:  kar-NOH, French: [kaʁno]), also called Carnot's rule or Carnot's law, is a principle of thermodynamics developed by Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot in 1824 that specifies limits on the maximum efficiency that any heat engine can obtain.
Carnot's theorem states that all heat engines operating between the same two thermal or heat reservoirs cannot have efficiencies greater than a reversible heat engine operating between the same reservoirs.

title: Carnot heat engine
intro: A Carnot heat engine (English:  kar-NOH, French: [kaʁno]) is a theoretical heat engine that operates on the Carnot cycle. The basic model for this engine was developed by French military engineer Nicolas Léonard Sadi Carnot in 1824.

title: Carpenter's rule problem
intro: The carpenter's rule problem is a discrete geometry problem, which can be stated in the following manner: Can a simple planar polygon be moved continuously to a position where all its vertices are in convex position, so that the edge lengths and simplicity are preserved along the way? A closely related problem is to show that any non-self-crossing polygonal chain can be straightened, again by a continuous transformation that preserves edge distances and avoids crossings.

title: Cartier-Brébeuf National Historic Site
intro: Cartier-Brébeuf National Historic Site (French: Site historique national Cartier-Brébeuf) is a National Historic Site of Canada and so designated by the Historic Sites and Monuments board of Canada in 1958 under the recommendation of  John Diefenbaker, the Prime Minister of Canada at the time. It is administered by Parks Canada and located at the confluence of Saint-Charles and Lairet rivers, in Quebec City, Quebec, Canada, more precisely in La Cité-Limoilou borough.

title: Casey's theorem
intro: In mathematics, Casey's theorem, also known as the generalized Ptolemy's theorem, is a theorem in Euclidean geometry named after the Irish mathematician John Casey. In Wasan, it is said to have been discovered roughly thirty years before Casey’s publication.
